question: A lucky year is one in which at least one date, when written in the form month/day/year, has the following property: the product of the month times the day equals the last two digits of the year. For example, \(1956\) is a lucky year because it has the date \(7/8/56\) and \(7 \times 8 = 56.\) Which of the following is NOT a lucky year?
solution:
A lucky year needs just one valid date. For \(1990,1991,1992,1993\), respectively, the dates \(5/18/90\), \(7/13/91\), \(4/23/92\), and \(3/31/93\) work because
\[
\begin{aligned}
5\times18&=90, &7\times13&=91,\\
4\times23&=92, &3\times31&=93.
\end{aligned}
\]
All four dates are valid, so those years are lucky.

For \(1994\), we need a month and day whose product is \(94\). To find every factor pair, put the smaller factor first. It must be less than \(10\), since two factors at least \(10\) would have product at least \(100\). Testing \(1\) through \(9\) gives only
\[
94=1\times94=2\times47.
\]
In both pairs, one factor exceeds \(31\). It cannot be a month, which is at most \(12\), or a day, which is at most \(31\). Therefore \(1994\) is not a lucky year, choice E.
